title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Mid-Barataria diversion budget set aside about $400 million to offset harm to fishers and communities

Oyster harvesters said it wasn't enough, and they had a point. Any coast plan has to make those who work the water whole, not treat them as collateral.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
BP agreed to a settlement of about $20.8 billion in 2015 over the Deepwater Horizon spill, the largest in Justice Department history

The biggest environmental settlement ever. That money was meant to repair the Gulf. With the diversion canceled, residents should watch where every dollar lands.

Source: U.S. Department of Justice, 2015 (via World Oil)

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
A federal judge found about 3.19 million barrels of oil spilled into the Gulf from Deepwater Horizon

Millions of barrels in our water, our marsh and our seafood. Eleven workers died on the rig. The cleanup was never just about money. It was about accountability.

Source: U.S. District Court, E.D. Louisiana, 2015

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Grand Isle, Louisiana, has a relative sea level rise trend of about 9.24 mm per year, roughly 3 feet per century

Grand Isle sits on sinking ground while the Gulf rises. That double squeeze makes it one of the fastest-changing shorelines in the country. It's a preview, not an outlier.

Source: NOAA Tides and Currents

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Galveston, Texas, shows relative sea level rising about 2.1 feet per century, while Pensacola, Florida, shows about 0.7 feet

Same Gulf, different fates. Sinking land along the Louisiana and Texas coasts makes the rise far worse there. Policy has to match the place.

Source: NOAA Tides and Currents

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The 2025 Gulf dead zone measured about 4,402 square miles

Smaller than many years, still bigger than Delaware and Rhode Island combined. In that water, fish and shrimp can't breathe. Shrimpers feel it in empty nets.

Source: NOAA, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Gulf dead zone's five-year average was about 4,755 square miles in 2025, versus a goal of under 1,900 by 2035

The official target is less than half of today's size. Without real limits on fertilizer runoff upriver, the goal stays a wish.

Source: NOAA / Hypoxia Task Force, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Isle de Jean Charles has lost about 98% of its land since 1955

A whole community's ground, nearly gone in one lifetime. Families who fished and trapped there for generations had to plan a move. That's what land loss looks like up close.

Source: State of Louisiana, reported by Houma Times, 2022

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The first residents of Isle de Jean Charles moved to The New Isle, a 515-acre site about 40 miles north, in August 2022

A $48 million federal grant built new homes inland. Some families moved; others stayed. Relocation should be a choice backed by real support, never a last resort forced by neglect.

Source: Houma Times, 2022

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The EPA and Justice Department sued Denka over chloroprene emissions in LaPlace in February 2023 and dropped the case in March 2025

Two years of federal action, then a reversal. The government said the case overreached in the name of environmental justice. Denka has denied its emissions endangered residents. LaPlace families are still waiting for clean air.

Source: Manufacturing Dive, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Denka suspended chloroprene production at its LaPlace plant indefinitely in May 2025, citing a roughly $112 million loss largely tied to emissions compliance costs

The company blamed regulation. Neighbors blamed decades of pollution. Either way, the workers lost shifts and the community lost certainty. A real transition plans for both.

Source: Manufacturing Dive, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
A July 2025 presidential proclamation gave 12 Louisiana chemical plants two-year exemptions from EPA's updated HON air toxics rule

The rule was written to cut cancer-causing emissions near homes. Twelve Louisiana plants, including Denka and DuPont in LaPlace, got a pass. Exemptions protect balance sheets, not lungs.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Army Corps of Engineers ordered a full environmental review of Formosa's St. James plastics plant in 2021

That review stalled the Sunshine Project for years. Formosa says its permits were properly issued and it remains committed. Residents who organized are the reason the review happened at all.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
An April 2025 IEEFA report recommended Formosa abandon its St. James project, citing an oversupplied plastics market

Even financial analysts say the plant doesn't make sense. Residents said it first. When the money and the neighbors agree, listen.

Source: Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, 2025 (via Louisiana Illuminator)

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
About 52,000 Louisianans dropped NFIP flood policies after Risk Rating 2.0, according to a 2024 report

Families didn't decide floods stopped. They decided they couldn't pay. Every dropped policy is a house that may never rebuild after the next storm.

Source: Office of U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy, 2024

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
About 80% of Louisiana NFIP policyholders saw premium increases under Risk Rating 2.0

Eight in ten. That's not a few high-risk mansions. That's working families across the state paying more for the same protection.

Source: Office of U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy, 2024

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
A standardized Louisiana homeowners policy cost about $5,400 in 2024, up more than 40% from 2021

That's a second mortgage payment for some families. When insurance costs more than taxes, people get pushed out of homes they own outright.

Source: Climate and Community Institute, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Standardized homeowners premiums reached as high as $14,400 a year in parts of south Louisiana in 2024

$14,400 a year, more than a month's wages for many workers. That price drives families off the coast without a single storm.

Source: Climate and Community Institute, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
59% of Louisiana homeowners would need more than 10% of their income for a standard policy in 2024, up from 48% in 2021

A majority now face a crushing insurance burden. That's a market failure, and a market failure needs a public answer.

Source: Climate and Community Institute, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana Citizens, the state insurer of last resort, more than tripled its policies from 2021 to 2022

When private companies fled after the storms, the public picked up the risk. If the public carries the risk, the public should set fair rules.

Source: Climate and Community Institute, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
FEMA announced the end of its BRIC disaster mitigation program on April 4, 2025

BRIC paid for prevention: drainage, elevation, stronger power lines. Ending it doesn't stop disasters. It just makes them more expensive.

Source: Congressional Research Service, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana had about $721 million in BRIC disaster mitigation funding at stake when the program was ended

Baton Rouge drainage, Ascension power lines, Coushatta evacuation routes, a New Orleans stormwater park. Real projects for real neighborhoods, frozen.

Source: WWNO, 2025

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
A federal court ruled in December 2025 that the termination of BRIC was unlawful and issued a permanent injunction

The courts said the cut broke the law. Now the fight is making sure the money actually reaches the ground before the next storm.

Source: Congressional Research Service, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Only about 21.6% of BRIC funds selected for FY2020 to FY2023 had been obligated as of March 2026

Billions promised, a fraction delivered. Prevention money that sits in Washington doesn't stop a single flood.

Source: Congressional Research Service, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana counted 26 Hurricane Ida storm-related deaths by mid-September 2021, with at least 10 from heat after power losses

Many Ida victims died after the wind stopped, in hot homes without power. A sturdier grid and cooling help would have saved lives.

Source: Louisiana Department of Health, via Louisiana Illuminator, 2021

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
At least 6 of Louisiana's early Hurricane Ida deaths were from carbon monoxide poisoning

Generators running in closed spaces kill after every storm. Safe backup power and cooling centers are basic public safety.

Source: Louisiana Department of Health, via Louisiana Illuminator, 2021

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana attributed 25 deaths to Hurricane Laura within about two weeks of landfall in 2020

Laura hit Southwest Louisiana with Category 4 winds. Many deaths came after the storm, from heat, generators and cleanup. Recovery is where policy saves or loses lives.

Source: Louisiana Department of Health, via KNOE, 2020

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The U.S. recorded 2,391 heat-related deaths in 2024

More than six heat deaths a day, every day, for a year. Heat is the deadliest weather most people never think about. The Gulf South lives in it.

Source: CDC, NCHS, MMWR QuickStats, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Adults aged 65 to 74 made up the largest share, about 21%, of U.S. heat-related deaths in 2024

Our parents and grandparents are on the front line of heat. No utility shutoffs in a heat wave should be the floor.

Source: CDC, NCHS, MMWR QuickStats, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Explicit fossil fuel subsidies worldwide reached about $1.3 trillion in 2022, up from about $500 billion in 2020

This is the direct kind: price caps, tax breaks and bill rebates. Counting hidden pollution costs too, the IMF total reached about $7 trillion. Either way, polluters get help working people don't.

Source: IMF, 2023

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The U.S. had about 8.5 million energy jobs in 2024, about 5.4% of all jobs

Energy is one of the country's biggest employers. The work is shifting fast. Louisiana's workers should shape where it goes.

Source: U.S. Department of Energy, 2025 USEER

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Wind and solar made up nearly 54% of U.S. electric power generation jobs in 2024

More than half of the people making electricity work in wind and solar. The jobs are already here. Louisiana just isn't getting its share.

Source: U.S. Department of Energy, 2025 USEER

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The 2025 budget law requires wind and solar projects to begin construction by July 4, 2026, or be placed in service by the end of 2027 to keep federal tax credits

A hard deadline killed projects before they started. Fewer projects mean fewer jobs and higher power bills for families.

Source: One Big Beautiful Bill Act, 2025 (via Kirkland & Ellis)

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
U.S. LNG exports averaged about 15 billion cubic feet per day in 2025, making the U.S. the world's largest LNG exporter

A huge share leaves from Louisiana. The gas goes overseas, the profits go to shareholders, and the storm risk stays in Cameron and Plaquemines parishes.

Source: EIA, via Journal of Petroleum Technology, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's job growth was under 1% over the last dozen years, compared with about 11.5% nationally

Decades of betting on oil and gas booms haven't built steady growth. Louisiana workers deserve an economy that doesn't crash every time prices fall.

Source: The Data Center, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
RWE agreed in August 2026 to relinquish its U.S. offshore wind leases, including one off Louisiana, in a $1.22 billion settlement with the Interior Department

Louisiana's first offshore wind lease is gone. Our fabricators and shipyards could have built it. That's jobs handed away.

Source: RWE / Marine Log, 2026

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Why is the Gulf Coast called a sacrifice zone?

Because somebody decided it could be spent. They cut canals through our marsh, stacked plants along our river, and drilled our Gulf. The profits went north. The land loss, the dirty air and the storm bills stayed here. That's not geography. That's policy. And policy can change.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
How fast did Louisiana lose land at its worst?

In the worst years, around the 1970s, USGS says we lost about 32 square miles a year. That's a football field about every 34 minutes. It has slowed, partly because we went years without a major hurricane. Slower isn't safe. It's a pause, not a rescue.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Did the oil companies cause the land loss?

Not all of it. Levees starving the delta of river mud, subsidence and storms all play a part. But a federal study for the Minerals Management Service found canals and spoil banks were tied to at least 30 to 60 percent of wetland loss from 1955 to 1978. They cut the coast open. They should help sew it back.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What happened to the Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion?

The state killed it in July 2025. It was a nearly $3 billion project paid for with BP spill settlement money, meant to rebuild land with river sediment. Oystermen and Plaquemines Parish sued against it, and their fears were real. But canceling it without a plan just as big means the marsh keeps sinking. Fishers and the coast both deserve a real plan, not a shrug.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Were the oystermen wrong to fight the diversion?

No. Freshwater would have hurt oyster beds, and $400 million for mitigation didn't feel like enough to people whose living was on the line. Their fight was fair. The failure is that the state made fishers and land-building into enemies. A just transition pays the people who carry the cost of saving the coast.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What does the Louisiana Coastal Master Plan say will happen if we do nothing?

The 2023 plan says we could lose about 1,100 more square miles by 2070, and as much as 3,000 if seas rise fast. More than 2 million people would face storm surge risk. Up to $15 billion in damage a year. The plan costs about $50 billion over 50 years. Doing nothing costs more.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
How fast is the sea rising at Grand Isle?

NOAA's tide gauge at Grand Isle shows relative sea level rising about 9 millimeters a year. That's around 3 feet a century, one of the fastest rates in the country. The land sinks and the water rises at the same time. Grand Isle feels both.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What's the dead zone?

Every summer, a patch of the Gulf runs so low on oxygen that fish and shrimp flee or die. In 2025 NOAA measured it at about 4,400 square miles. Fertilizer runoff from up the Mississippi feeds it. Farmers upriver and fishers down here both get squeezed while agribusiness skips the bill.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Is the dead zone getting better?

2025 was smaller than average, and that's good news. But the five-year average is still about 4,755 square miles. The official goal is under 1,900 by 2035. We're not close. One good year is weather. Hitting the goal takes policy.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What happened to the Denka lawsuit?

In February 2023 the EPA and Justice Department sued Denka over chloroprene from its LaPlace plant, saying the cancer risk for neighbors was too high. In March 2025 the government dropped the case. Denka has long denied its emissions endangered residents. Then in May 2025 it suspended production, blaming compliance costs. The neighbors were never the ones who got a pause.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What is the HON rule exemption?

In 2024 EPA tightened pollution limits on chemical plants, including cancer-causing gases like ethylene oxide and chloroprene. In July 2025 a presidential proclamation gave two-year exemptions to plants, including 12 in Louisiana, among them Denka and DuPont in LaPlace. The rule was written for us. The exemption was written for them.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Is the Formosa plant in St. James being built?

Not yet. The Sunshine Project has been stalled for years. The Army Corps ordered a full environmental review in 2021, and that takes time. Formosa says it is still committed. A 2025 IEEFA report told the company to walk away. St. James residents fought this every step. That's why it's still a field.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Why did so many Louisianans drop flood insurance?

Risk Rating 2.0. FEMA's new pricing started in 2021 and premiums climbed year after year. Senator Cassidy's office reported about 52,000 Louisianans dropped their policies and 80 percent saw increases. People didn't stop needing flood insurance. They stopped being able to pay for it. That's how the next storm turns into the next ruin.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Why is homeowners insurance crushing Louisiana families?

A 2025 report from the Climate and Community Institute found a standard policy cost about $5,400 in 2024, with some south Louisiana homes facing up to $14,400. Most homeowners would need more than a tenth of their income to cover it. Insurers left after the 2020 and 2021 storms. The state's insurer of last resort more than tripled. We're paying private prices for public risk.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What happened to FEMA's BRIC program?

BRIC paid for flood walls, drainage and stronger grids before disasters hit. In April 2025 FEMA ended it. Louisiana had about $721 million on the line. In December 2025 a federal court ruled the termination unlawful. Prevention is cheaper than recovery. Cutting it isn't saving money. It's moving the bill to the next storm.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Who died in Hurricane Ida?

In Louisiana, many of the dead didn't drown. By mid-September 2021, the state counted 26 storm-related deaths, and at least 17 were tied to losing power: 10 from heat and 6 from carbon monoxide. The storm knocked out the lights. The grid we were sold let the heat finish the job.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What happened to the nursing home residents during Ida?

About 800 nursing home residents were moved into one warehouse in Tangipahoa Parish. Conditions broke down and residents died after the evacuation. The state shut those homes down. Old people are not freight. Every evacuation plan should be public, inspected and enforced.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
How many people die from heat in America?

CDC counted 2,391 heat-related deaths in 2024. The biggest share was people 65 to 74. Workers outside and elders without AC are on the front line. Heat is the quiet killer of the Gulf South. Shade, water and power are life and death.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Are fossil fuels really subsidized?

Yes, and be precise. The IMF counted about $1.3 trillion in explicit fossil fuel subsidies worldwide in 2022, things like price caps and bill rebates. Add the implicit costs, mostly unpaid pollution damage, and the total hit about $7 trillion. Explicit is cash and price breaks. Implicit is the bill they leave on our lungs.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What happened to clean energy credits in 2025?

The July 2025 budget law cut them hard. Wind and solar projects now have to start construction by July 4, 2026, or be running by the end of 2027, or lose the credit. The home solar credit ended after 2025. Louisiana families lost a way to cut power bills, and workers lost jobs before they started.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
How many energy jobs are there in America?

The 2025 DOE energy jobs report counted about 8.5 million energy jobs in 2024, about 5.4 percent of all jobs. Wind and solar made up nearly 54 percent of jobs in electric power generation. The work is shifting. The question is whether Gulf workers get a seat or a pink slip.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Isn't the LNG boom good for Louisiana?

It's big. The U.S. became the world's largest LNG exporter, around 15 billion cubic feet a day in 2025, and Louisiana terminals carry much of it. Construction jobs are real. But a plant takes thousands to build and far fewer to run. Gas leaves our ports and the profits leave our state. The flares and the storm risk stay with Cameron Parish.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What does a just transition mean for an oil worker?

It means you don't get thrown away. Wage guarantees, pensions protected, health care kept, first hire for coastal restoration, plugging orphan wells, building grid and wind. Your skills built this industry. They can rebuild this coast. The plan has to be written with you, not about you.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Are there really enough jobs restoring the coast?

The Master Plan is roughly $50 billion over 50 years. Since 2005 Louisiana has spent about $21.4 billion on more than 140 coastal projects. That's dredging, pipelines, heavy equipment and engineering. Our workers already know how to move mud and lay pipe. Fund it steady and it's a career, not a gig.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What's the deal with abandoned wells in coastal Louisiana?

From 1901 to 2017 there were 76,247 drilling permits in 14 coastal parishes, according to LSU research. Tens of thousands of those spots ended dry or abandoned. Fewer than about 50 were filled back in. Companies took the oil and left the holes. Plugging and restoring them is work our people can do, paid by the people who drilled.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What happened to Isle de Jean Charles?

The island has lost about 98 percent of its land since 1955. In August 2022 the first families moved to The New Isle, about 40 miles north, built with a $48 million HUD grant. Some went, some stayed. Nobody should have to choose between home and safety because the marsh was sold off.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Who paid for the Deepwater Horizon damage?

BP agreed to a settlement of about $20.8 billion in 2015, the largest in Justice Department history. A federal judge found about 3.19 million barrels spilled. Eleven workers died. That money was supposed to rebuild the coast. When the state cancels the biggest project it was meant for, people should ask where it goes next.

title: Claude Drop: climate-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What happened to offshore wind off Louisiana?

Louisiana held the first Gulf offshore wind lease. In August 2026 RWE agreed with the Interior Department to give up its leases, including Louisiana's, in a $1.22 billion settlement. Our shipyards and fabricators built offshore oil. They could have built offshore wind. That door got shut in Washington, not here.
